text:
Oh, fierce love, you came like the butterfly

that approaches the rose when October begins;

everything was silence, open silence

to mysterious shadows like a dead man's eye.


I was the same shadow, I was less, I was

a sleeping thing that neither dreams nor hopes,

when the flight of that celestial butterfly

suddenly made me warble like a wild bird.


Oh, a hundred suns rose in the east,

oh, a hundred rivers ran down the same slope,

oh, a hundred silver moons shone in the sky,

and a hundred high mountains took flight.


I opened my arms: I had the divine madness

of touching the things of the heights with my fingers.

I opened my eyes: I had the divine sadness

of drinking celestial beauty with my eyes.


I wept, I wept without cease; I cried: My heart,

stop on the road that leads to delirium;

but my heart was a drop of wax...

God, what could that drop do against spring?...


Fierce love: into your hands I have released my life;

receive it: a Dove that settles, exhausted,

in bloodstained claws no longer beats its wings:

it dies from what it lives on; it lives from what you exhale.


I know well that no hundred suns are born in the east,

I know well that no hundred rivers run down one slope,

I know well that no hundred moons shine in the sky,

I know well that no mountains lengthen into flight.


I know well that doves blind their eyes, leave

their feathers in the nest, and dawns draw away,

leaves fall, autumn comes, death,

days turn gray, and fortune turns gray.


But I am a slave to pain and adore it

as the miser adores the sound of gold:

oh, terrible storm of lightning and thunder,

in your fire I revive, in your fire I faint.


Fierce love: I am small as a snowflake,

fierce love: I am small as a little bird,

sad as the moan of a dying child,

fierce love, you would find no better prey in the world.


No one would die more lightly in your claws,

no one would die sooner in your bonds.

Shine, rising sun... Nature, grow:

over dark life, death shines.

translation.title: Fierce Love
translation.editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem’s deliberate multiplication of suns, rivers, moons, and mountains, then returns to ordinary seasonal mortality.
